1.title: Scrum Definition, Theory and Empiricism
1.text: Welcome to Module 1: Scrum Definition, Theory and Empiricism. This is the foundation for everything else in the course. You will learn what Scrum is, why it works, and what a team loses when it uses only some of it. Pay special attention to the three pillars, because they are easy to mix up with the values.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Define Scrum in your own words. Explain empiricism and lean thinking. Name the three pillars and how they depend on each other. Give benefits of working iteratively and incrementally. Explain why partial Scrum is not Scrum, and what it costs. And spot the classic traps: pillars versus values, and framework versus method.

1.title: Case Check-In: A Plan for the Year
1.text: Back at RideLoop. Grace Whitfield, the Director of Operations, asks for a detailed plan, with dates, for the next twelve months. You explain that the team plans one Sprint at a time, and learns from each Increment. Then there is a second story. In Sprint six, the team skipped the Retrospective to save time. The same complaint about the slow station map then came back twice. One story is about empiricism. The other is about leaving parts of Scrum out.

1.title: Scrum in One Sentence
1.text: Start with the definition. The Guide says Scrum is "a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems." Let us unpack it. Lightweight framework: few rules, and purposely incomplete. People, teams and organizations: Scrum serves all three levels. Generate value: the aim is value, not output. Adaptive solutions: the team learns and adjusts as it goes. Complex problems: work whose results cannot be fully predicted. For the exam, remember that Scrum is a framework, not a detailed method.

1.title: Scrum in a Nutshell
1.text: Here is Scrum in a nutshell. First, a Product Owner puts the work in order in the Product Backlog. Next, the Scrum Team picks some of that work and, within a Sprint, turns it into an Increment: a usable step toward the goal. Then the team and its stakeholders, the people with an interest in the product, look at the result together and decide what to change. After that, it starts again. A Scrum Master looks after the environment in which all of this happens.

1.title: A Framework, Not a Method
1.text: Scrum is a framework, not a method. The Guide calls it purposely incomplete: it defines only the parts the theory needs. Its rules guide relationships and interactions, rather than giving detailed instructions. Other techniques can be used inside it, and Scrum wraps around existing practices or makes some of them unnecessary. So how to estimate, how to write requirements and how to test are the team's choices, not Scrum's. The Guide invites you to try Scrum as it is, and judge by the results. If an exam option says that Scrum prescribes one of these techniques, it is wrong.

1.title: Scrum Theory: Empiricism and Lean Thinking
1.text: Scrum theory rests on two ideas. Empiricism: knowledge comes from experience, and decisions rest on what is observed. And lean thinking: reduce waste and focus on the essentials. A note on wording. The earlier edition of the Guide talked about empirical process control, and called Scrum difficult to master. The current Guide uses empiricism and lean thinking. If a question offers both, answer with empiricism and lean thinking.

1.title: Complex Work: Only the Past Informs the Future
1.text: Why empiricism? Because Scrum is built for complex work, where outcomes cannot be known in advance. Decisions about the future can use only what has already happened. Compare the two styles. Up-front prediction plans everything, then follows the plan. It treats change as an exception, judges progress against the plan, and handles risk at the start. Empiricism plans a little, learns, and plans again. It expects new information, judges progress by the inspected Increment, and limits risk in every short cycle. Burn-down charts and similar forecasts are useful, but they do not replace empiricism: only what has already happened should drive forward-looking decisions. That is also your answer to Grace's twelve-month plan.

1.title: The Three Pillars
1.text: The three pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation. Transparency: the work is visible to those doing it and to those receiving it. Inspection: the artifacts and progress are checked frequently and diligently, and the five events give the rhythm. Adaptation: when something goes outside acceptable limits, adjust as soon as possible. Do not confuse these with the values. Commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage are values, not pillars.

1.title: What Goes Wrong Without a Pillar
1.text: The pillars form a chain: transparency enables inspection, and inspection enables adaptation. Break the chain and see what goes wrong. Without transparency, inspection is misleading and wasteful, and decisions can diminish value and increase risk. Without adaptation, inspection is pointless, because the events are designed to provoke change. Slow adaptation lets deviation grow, so adapt as soon as possible. And adapting is harder when people are not empowered. In a question, look for the answer that keeps the chain intact.

1.title: Iterative and Incremental
1.text: Scrum works iteratively and incrementally. Iterative means repeating cycles, and using what you learned to improve the next one. Incremental means building the product in usable slices, each added to the earlier ones. A Sprint is both: it repeats the inspect and adapt cycle, and it produces an Increment. The Sprint is also the container that holds the other four events. The Guide's aim for this approach is to optimize predictability and to control risk.

1.title: Benefits of Working This Way
1.text: The Guide names two aims: predictability and risk control. The benefits usually taught for this learning objective go a little further, so this slide carries the tag Beyond the Guide. Earlier feedback, because stakeholders inspect a real Increment every Sprint. Earlier value, from the first Sprints. Lower risk, because each Sprint limits cost and effort. Better predictability, because progress is checked at least every month. Response to change, because the Product Backlog can be reordered. And continuous learning, because every Retrospective feeds the next Sprint. If asked, name at least three.

1.title: Scrum Is Immutable
1.text: Scrum is immutable. The Guide says that using only parts of Scrum is possible, but "the result is not Scrum." Scrum exists only in its entirety, and each element serves a purpose that is essential to its value. Leaving elements out covers up problems and limits the benefits. At the same time, Scrum is a container: you may add techniques inside it. Adding is fine; removing parts is not. When a team skips a part, the best answer restores it and explains what it protects. The diagram shows it: techniques fit inside the container, but take the Retrospective out and it is not Scrum anymore.

1.title: Disadvantages of Partial Scrum
1.text: What do you lose when a part is left out? No Retrospective: the same problems repeat, as at RideLoop. No Definition of Done: nobody knows what done means, and quality drifts. No Sprint Review: feedback arrives late. No single Product Owner: priorities become unclear. No fixed-length Sprints: the regular rhythm of inspection and adaptation is lost. No Scrum Master: Scrum erodes back into old habits. Overall, problems stay hidden, and a team can call itself Scrum without getting Scrum's results. The Guide does not list these consequences, so they go beyond it; they show why leaving a part out costs a team.

1.title: Traps: What the Exam Expects
1.text: Here are the traps. Pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation. Values are commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. Scrum is a framework, and technique choices belong to the team. Empiricism means decisions from observation, never from early detailed prediction. Adapt as soon as possible, because inspection without adaptation is pointless. Partial Scrum is not Scrum, so restore what is missing. Scrum is not only for software: the Guide uses the word developers for everyone who does the work. And keep the numbers apart: five events, three artifacts, three commitments, three accountabilities, three pillars, five values.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Recap. Scrum is a lightweight framework for generating value from complex work. Its theory is empiricism and lean thinking. The pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation, in a chain. The approach is iterative and incremental, to optimize predictability and control risk. Partial Scrum is not Scrum, and it costs you hidden problems and lost benefits. Now test yourself with five questions.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Grace Whitfield asks why the RideLoop team cannot plan the whole year in detail and then follow the plan. Which explanation of Scrum is best? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. In complex work what will happen is unknown, so decisions rest on what has been observed: plan a little, inspect the result and adapt. The other options contradict the theory or the scope of the framework.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Stakeholders say they cannot tell what the RideLoop team has really finished, because many items are almost done. Which pillar is weak, and what helps most? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. Transparency means the work is visible and everyone shares one understanding of what is finished, and the Definition of Done provides that. Reports and meetings do not, and courage is a value, not a pillar.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Grace suggests that whenever items are late, the Sprint should simply run until they are finished. What is the best response from the Scrum Master? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Partial Scrum is not Scrum. Sprints have a fixed length to give a regular chance to inspect and adapt. The Scrum Master helps people understand why, instead of policing them.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which three are the empirical pillars of Scrum? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A: transparency, inspection and adaptation. Option B lists values, option C mixes a value with a pillar, and option D lists events.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which of these is a benefit of working iteratively and incrementally? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. Short cycles limit cost and effort, so the cost of being wrong stays small. The other options describe the opposite of Scrum: a fixed scope, late feedback, and plans that never change.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: B. Complex work needs empiricism. Question two: C. Transparency means visible work and a shared meaning of Done. Question three: D. Partial Scrum is not Scrum. Question four: A. The pillars are transparency, inspection and adaptation. Question five: C. Short cycles keep risk low. That completes Module 1. Next, Module 2 covers the Scrum values and the Agile Manifesto.
